1.pericope_label: It is superfluous to write; the brethren sent before to prepare your bounty

schools.summary: Do not let the chapter break mislead the reader: there is no new subject here, only the continuation of an appeal to self-respect begun a few verses earlier. Then handle the two loaded words. The term rendered confidence means literally that which stands under, a base or ground, and the papyri use it commonly for property; it has a long later history in theological controversy, appearing as person in one place of Hebrews and substance in another. The term rendered bounty means blessing, and its later career is worth tracing -- the consecrated bread and wine, then the portions reserved for the sick and absent, then the unconsecrated remains, and at last gifts of bread to friends or the poor. Note the rhetoric plainly as well. The writing Paul calls superfluous he nonetheless does; Macedonians stands without the article so as to rouse an esprit de corps; the turn by which he says we, that we say not ye, should be ashamed is as fine as anything in the best classical writers. And say what was at stake: Paul had boasted of Corinth to move the Macedonians, so a failure now would touch his veracity and their character together.

Meet head-on the suspicion that Paul does not mean what he says. If he thinks them prepared he need not admonish; if he doubts them he should not call admonition unnecessary. The answer is that love carries both, good hope and anxious concern. He had seen a happy commencement and expected the progress to answer to it, but knowing the unsteadiness of the human mind he could not guard too carefully; and having pledged his own credit along with theirs by boasting everywhere of their liberality, he cannot refrain from speaking. Be exact about what he had claimed on their behalf: not that the money was already laid aside in the chest, but that it had been resolved upon, which involves no fickleness or mistake. Then define the collection itself, which is neither the ministry of the gospel nor the mutual assistance church members owe each other, but this contribution and their liberality in it. And give the two Greek words their weight: the one rendered bounty answers to the Hebrew for blessing, which covers both a prayer for another's prosperity and actual beneficence, while the one set against it covers both excessive greed and mere niggardliness, the paring off of what ought to be given.

Locate the danger in how the thing would look to outsiders. Had the Corinthians hung back, strangers would have imputed a covetous principle, as of men who part with money only when ashamed to keep it any longer, whereas readiness to give is the mark of a liberal mind; and bounty of that kind is not wrung by importunity from covetous persons. There is no need to hunt for some new sense of the word for covetousness to make this work. Fill in the geography while you are at it: Achaia anciently meant the whole Morea with Corinth for its capital, so churches beyond Corinth were involved, Cenchrea among them, and the collection would be drawn from all of them. Note the textual variant between notice given before and promise made before, without pretending the sense turns on it. And state the reason for sending the brethren without softening it -- Paul wished them to preserve the character he had given them, since otherwise he might be reputed a liar and both he and they be ashamed before the Macedonians.

Read the passage as a piece of skill and say so. The apostle speaks very respectfully and with great address: while he seems to excuse pressing them so earnestly, he presses them still, and by commending what they have already done he lays an obligation on them to go on. Take the first point as needless argument -- he was satisfied he had said enough already to prevail with men of whom he had so good an opinion, knowing their forwardness and having boasted of their zeal to the Macedonians, which had provoked many of them to do as Corinth had done. Then take the sending of Titus and the brethren as something he must almost apologize for, being unwilling they should think him too earnest or suspicious of them; and give the true reason, that having this timely notice they might be fully ready, and not surprised with hasty demands when he came.

Admire the craft and name the device. Though he had said so much about the collection already, and though he is about to say more, he calls it superfluous to write -- and this is the rhetorical figure of omission, which is very effective. A judge who sees the magnanimity of an accuser entertains no suspicion of him, reasoning that a man who could say much and does not is unlikely to invent what is not true. So here the effect is to win the hearers rather than press them. And observe the second edge of it: a man who has been given so high a reputation that he is said to need no advice is ashamed to appear inferior to that opinion of himself. Distinguish also what belongs to which part of the argument -- what was said a little above concerned those who were to receive the money, and what came before that, the account of the Macedonians whose deep poverty abounded to the riches of their liberality, concerned loving-kindness and almsgiving.

debates.question: Why does Paul call it superfluous to write and then write?

sides.position: It is the rhetorical figure of omission, effective because a hearer who sees what the speaker could have said and did not entertains no suspicion of him; and a man given so high a character as to need no advice is ashamed to fall short of it
The writing ought to be superfluous, and all the same he does write
There is no new subject here at all, the chapter division notwithstanding, only a continuation of the appeal to their self-respect
Love carries both good hope and anxious concern; he had seen a happy commencement but knowing the unsteadiness of the human mind could not guard too carefully

debates.question: What was at stake in sending the brethren ahead?

sides.position: Paul's veracity and their character together, since he had moved the Macedonians to give by boasting of Corinth and might be charged with trick if it failed
Their esprit de corps: Macedonians stands without the article, so that Achaians should not let Macedonians arrive and find them short of the account given
Nothing but timeliness, so that they should not be surprised with hasty demands when he came

outliers.note: Alone names the device by which the passage works, the rhetorical figure of omission, and explains its effect from the courtroom: a judge who sees that an accuser could have said much and did not entertains no suspicion of him.

Alone follows the word for bounty forward through its later ecclesiastical career, from the consecrated bread and wine to the portions reserved for the sick and absent, then the unconsecrated remains, and at last gifts of bread to friends or the poor.

themes: as touching the ministering to the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you
your zeal hath provoked very many
make up beforehand your bounty... that the same might be ready, as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness

6.pericope_label: He which soweth sparingly; God loveth a cheerful giver

schools.summary: Treat the sowing line as a proverb and work the figure out. Money given in alms resembles seed committed to the earth: it may lie buried long enough that one ignorant of providence would think it lost, and yet it springs up with ample increase. Then draw the limit the figure implies -- what a man reaps answers not to the quantity of the gift, except so far as quantity indicates character, but to the spirit in which it was given. On the verb for purposing, note that it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and carries the full ethical sense the moralists gave it, a settled resolve deciding both end and means, not a passing impulse or a half-regretted promise; it is a permanent purpose, in the perfect tense. Observe that the negative used with grudgingly requires an imperative to be supplied. Trace the cheerful giver clause to the Greek of Proverbs, where it differs markedly from the Hebrew -- evidence that Paul quoted habitually from that version, and, coming soon after another quotation from the same book, a sign that his mind was full of it. And note that the word behind cheerful is the ancestor of hilarious.

Give directions about the manner of giving, since it matters not only that we do what is required but that we do it as commanded. Three things: bountifully, deliberately, and freely. On the second, insist that works of charity, like other good works, should be done with thought and design, whereas some do good only by accident -- complying hastily with the importunity of others, giving more than they intended and repenting of it afterwards, or giving less than a proper consideration of their own circumstances and the case of the person relieved would have prompted. On the third, note how often what is given is in a manner squeezed or forced out to satisfy someone who asks, and that this unwillingness spoils the whole. Due deliberation about our means and the needs before us is the help we want in judging how liberal to be.

Press the seed figure on its unpromising side, since that is where the difficulty lies. The seed is cast out by the hand, scattered on this side and that, harrowed in, and rots, so that it seems as good as lost; and so the alms look like a diminishing of what you have, until the harvest comes. Make the doctrine into an instrument: when carnal reason holds us back through fear of loss, lift this shield, that the Lord reckons what is laid out on the poor as lent to himself and repays it with interest, in this world as well as in heaven. Then guard the other side. Liberality is estimated by God not from the sum but from the disposition, and nothing is to be extorted from anyone against his will. Distinguish two necessities: the one we impose on ourselves in obeying God is compatible with willingness, since we may constrain a reluctant flesh and still act freely, while constraint from the influence of others leaves a man wishing he could avoid the duty. Alms are a sacrifice, and no sacrifice pleases God unless it is voluntary; He does not lord it over us as a tyrant but requires the cheerful obedience of children.

Show that the figure is not the apostle's invention: sowing was ordinary Jewish usage for almsgiving, and two prophetic passages were read that way -- blessed are ye that sow beside all waters, and sow to yourselves in almsgiving and reap in mercy. Then explain the pair of negatives from the temple furniture. There were two chests for alms, one for what the law required and one for free-will offerings; of those who gave to the first nothing is said, of those who gave to the second much is said, and it is to these two that the apostle alludes. Draw the consequence sharply: the benefit of almsgiving is lost to the giver who does it with a grumbling heart, and the mere performance of the letter of the law in that spirit is an abomination. State the rule itself in one line -- God proportions the reward to the work and to the temper it proceeds from -- and define giving of necessity as the state of a man who cannot tell how to refuse.

debates.question: Should giving be deliberated over or done on first impulse?

sides.position: Deliberated. Works of charity should be done with thought and design, whereas some do good only by accident, complying hastily with importunity and repenting of it after
Deliberated. The verb means a settled resolve deciding both end and means, not a passing impulse or a half-regretted promise

On first impulse. The heart is more concerned in giving than the head, and a man who deliberates too long lets avarice in and gives less than he first meant; man is too selfish to be in much danger of giving too much
The verse is not about amount at all, but about the manner of giving

debates.question: What lies behind the pair of negatives?

sides.position: The temple's two alms chests, one for what the law required and one for free-will offerings; nothing is said of those who gave to the first, much of those who gave to the second
Two kinds of necessity: the one we impose on ourselves in obeying God is compatible with willingness, while constraint from others leaves a man wishing he could avoid the duty

outliers.note: Alone argues against deliberation in giving, holding that the instinctive prompting of a benevolent heart is to give liberally and that a man who thinks too long lets avarice in, and defending the position on the ground that man at best is too selfish to be in much danger of giving too much.

Alone explains the pair of negatives from the temple furniture, the two alms chests for what the law required and for free-will offerings, of the first of which nothing is said and of the second much.

themes: He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity

8.pericope_label: God is able to make all grace abound; he hath dispersed abroad

schools.summary: Identify the word for sufficiency as a term of the Greek moralists, occurring only here and once in a later letter. Self-sufficiency was for them the crown of the perfect life, vindicated by Aristotle for happiness and constantly on Stoic lips in Paul's own day; so note the borrowing, but note the limit too -- Paul takes the ideal of independence from circumstances without the withdrawal from society the Cynics attached to it. Draw the practical line: what is promised is not the superfluity that ministers to selfish luxury but the competence disciples should be content with. Count the threefold all of the verse, and observe that the verb for is able is a late one found almost nowhere but in Paul. On the quotation, do not force it. It might at first seem to describe God dispersing his own bounty rather than the almsgiver, but the parallelism of the psalm settles it, wealth in the house answering to righteousness enduring, so that the man can keep giving from a store continually replenished. Or take Paul as citing part of a familiar passage and meaning the whole of it. And distinguish the word for the poor here, a man who works for his living, from the word for an abject beggar.

State the objection in the voice of the man who feels it: what is given away is so much the less left for yourself. Answer that we are by nature excessively niggardly because we are prone to distrust, which tempts every one to grasp what is his; and that those who do good to the poor provide for their own interest no less than a man watering his land, since alms work like canals to make the blessing of God flow back toward the giver. Be careful about the kind of power meant -- not the inert power of the poets, but the power Scripture ascribes to God, put forth in action, whose present efficacy we feel. Note the double provision in the promise: enough for themselves, and something over for doing good; and take sufficiency to mean the measure God knows to be useful, since it is not always profitable for us to be filled to satiety. On the psalm, read it of a liberality that flows unceasingly, as water from a perennial fountain, and connect it to the charge not to be weary in well-doing. Then work through what all grace does not mean before settling on what it does.

Keep the word grace in the sense this letter has been using, a charitable gift, so that the promise is of temporal good sufficient to let them abound in every good work -- the reaping that answers to sowing plenteously. Remark on the wording rather than hurrying past it: each word here is loaded with matter and increases all the way it goes, and all things in this life, rewards included, are to the faithful seeds for a future harvest. On the quotation, keep the sower in view. He scatters abroad, that is, not merely at home among those he knows but among strangers, whether of his own nation or another; he does it with a full hand, without an anxious thought which way each grain falls. And take righteousness in the sense the Jews gave it, beneficence together with its blessed effects, so that what remains for ever is the good deed and its fruit, the store unexhausted because God keeps renewing it.

debates.question: How does the quotation from the psalm support the argument?

sides.position: By taking righteousness in the sense the Jews gave it, beneficence, so that what endures for ever is the good deed and its effects
Not by that route. Paul cites part of a familiar passage while meaning the whole, which goes on to promise that the giver's horn shall be exalted with honour
By the parallelism of the psalm, where wealth in the house answers to righteousness enduring, so that the man can keep giving from a store continually replenished

A term of the Greek moralists, self-sufficiency being the crown of the perfect life for them; what is promised is not superfluity ministering to selfish luxury but the competence disciples should be content with
The same borrowing, but without the Cynic withdrawal from society that often accompanied it
The measure God knows to be useful, since it is not always profitable for us to be filled to satiety; and a double provision, enough for themselves and something over for doing good

outliers.note: Alone tests the promise against his own observation, reporting that he can hardly point to anyone impoverished by liberality while multitudes are made poor by the want of it, parsimonious in giving and extravagant in dress and amusement.

Alone distinguishes the kind of power meant, insisting that Paul speaks of it not as the poets do but as Scripture does, of a power put forth in action whose present efficacy is felt, and not an inactive power we merely imagine.

themes: God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work
He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor

10.pericope_label: He that ministereth seed to the sower; enriched to all bountifulness

schools.summary: Trace the verb rendered ministereth to its origin in the Greek theatre, where it meant to defray the cost of a chorus at one's own expense. Being an act of stately generosity the word widened to any such act, and Paul appears to be the first, so far as can be traced, to transfer it to the divine bounty; the Greek Old Testament barely uses it, and Peter takes it up later, possibly enriching his vocabulary from these letters. Note the scriptural echoes as well -- seed to the sower from Isaiah, with a different verb, and fruits of righteousness from Hosea and Amos. Correct the construction from the better manuscripts: he who bounteously gives seed to the sower and bread for food, God's beneficence being thought of in seed-time and harvest alike, shall give bounteously and multiply your seed and increase the produce of your righteousness. Settle the spelling of that last noun in favour of the form used of vegetable produce rather than the one used of animals. And admit the grammar for what it is -- the participles that follow are not connected to the preceding sentence, an independent use whose meaning is nonetheless plain. The context points primarily to temporal abundance, though the spiritual riches found in Christ can scarcely have been absent from his mind.

Decide first whether these words are promise or prayer, because the manuscripts differ. Some put the three verbs in the future, which would make the sentence a restatement of what has just been promised, and Paul does repeat a promise in different words to fix it in men's minds. Others give the infinitive, which can stand for an optative; prefer that, both as the more generally received reading and because Paul habitually follows his exhortations with prayer for what he has just taught. Then say what the circumlocution is doing. Sowing looks like the fountainhead from which food flows, so that the husbandman seems to support himself and others by his own effort; naming God as the one who supplies seed to the sower denies exactly that, as Moses denied it when he warned Israel against saying that their own hand had gotten them their wealth. On the enriching, call the contented mind the true affluence, since nothing is more famished than the distrustful, who are tormented with an anxious desire of having; and note that the alms have a further end, the glory of God and the thanksgiving of those relieved.

Take the same theatrical origin for the verb but press a different sense from it -- one who leads up the chorus, and so one who furnishes one thing after another so that there is no want or chasm, which is exactly how providence connects causes with effects. Then argue from creation. Had God not made every plant with its seed in itself, no harvest could have come without a previous sowing, and there would have been no seed to put in the ground; so too, had he not given them their property, almsgiving would be impossible, and without his blessing riches take wings and flee away. Since all of it comes from him, he has the right to require that it be dispensed as he judges best. Then ask the blunt questions and answer them. Why does God give riches? That they may be applied to his glory and the good of men. Why does he increase them? That those who have them may exercise all bountifulness. And if they do not, the rust will canker them and the moth consume their garments. Define the terms simply as you go: seed is opportunity and ability to help others, bread is what is needful for soul and body, and the fruits of righteousness are the happy effects of love to God and man.

Show the reader the architecture of the argument. Having exhorted from spiritual considerations and from temporal, Paul does the very same with the recompense, setting the two kinds continually side by side -- he hath scattered abroad belongs to a spiritual return, multiply your seed to a temporal, increase the fruits of your righteousness to a spiritual again. He does this to give variety to the discourse and to tear up by the roots their unmanly and faint-hearted reasoning, using many arguments to dissipate the fear of poverty. Then supply the argument from the lesser to the greater: if God gives to those who sow the earth, and grants abundance to those who feed the body, much more will he give to those who till the soil of heaven and take care for the soul, since these are the ones he wills should enjoy his providing care. And notice the form. He does not state it as an inference but as a prayer, which at once makes his meaning plain and leads them on to hope, not only from what commonly happens but from his own praying; and the words multiply and increase hint, in a way that rouses no suspicion, at largeness in the giving.

debates.question: Is this sentence a promise or a prayer?

sides.position: A prayer. Some manuscripts give the verbs in the future, but the infinitive reading is more generally received, and Paul habitually follows exhortation with prayer for what he has taught
A prayer, and deliberately so: he states it not as an inference but in the form of a prayer, which makes his meaning plain and leads them on to hope from his praying
The expression of an earnest wish that they might experience in themselves what had been stated as a rule

debates.question: What does the verb behind ministereth carry with it?

sides.position: The chorus-leader of the Greek stage who furnished a chorus at his own expense, which widened into supplying generally
The same origin, with a history: an act of stately generosity, barely used in the Greek Old Testament, transferred by Paul apparently first of all to the divine bounty, and taken up later by Peter
The same origin but a different force: one who furnishes one thing after another so that there is no want or chasm, which is how providence connects causes with effects

outliers.note: Alone describes the architecture of the argument, that Paul sets a spiritual return and a temporal one continually side by side in order to give variety to the discourse and to tear up by the roots their faint-hearted reasoning about poverty.

Alone argues the point from creation, that had God not made every plant with its seed in itself there could have been no seed to sow, and concludes that since the property is his gift he has the right to require how it be dispensed.

themes: he that ministereth seed to the sower both minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed sown
increase the fruits of your righteousness
Being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God

12.pericope_label: The administration of this service; their prayer for you

schools.summary: Give the word for this service its history, since our word liturgy is the same word. It is built from the terms for people and work, and covers public service whether rendered to God in worship or to others in benefaction. In classical Greek it stands for any public service to the State; in the Greek Old Testament it is used almost exclusively of the ritual and sacrificial services of tabernacle and temple; and in the ecclesiastical vocabulary it was applied at first only to the celebration of the Lord's Supper. Draw the conclusion that history suggests, that a large and liberal gift to Christ's poor is the most acceptable of all forms of service in the liturgical sense. Note that the verb means to fill up by adding to, the Corinthians supplying their part of a total already gathered elsewhere, and that the want being filled was urgent: the Jerusalem disciples had never quite recovered from the famine foretold by Agabus, and the lavish generosity of the first days had exhausted their resources. Prefer test to experiment for the next word, and correct the rendering of what follows -- not a professed subjection but an obedience to the confession of faith. Say plainly what the collection would prove: that Gentiles make as good Christians as Jews.

Explain the word for service from both directions. In the Greek Bible it belongs to the sacrifices and other duties of priests and Levites; among Greek writers it names a public office, and at Athens especially one discharged by the richer citizens at their own expense and in rotation, the burdensome and chargeable offices being laid on men of considerable estate. Then take the proof in the following verse as a genuine test: it was token enough of the Corinthians' love that they were liberal to brethren at a great distance from them, and the proof extends further, to their concurrent obedience to the gospel, since alms conferred by the common consent of all show that concurrence. Finally, note that the apostle omits no motive that might stir them. He has named the comfort believers would feel, the thanksgiving by which God would be glorified, and the public confession of their unanimity in faith; now he adds the return the saints will make, goodwill springing from gratitude and earnest prayer, so that those relieved have the means of requiting their benefactors.

Enumerate the effects of the gift in order, because the passage does. The wants of the saints are supplied; many thanksgivings are rendered to God; the Corinthians give proof of their subjection to the gospel; and the prayers of those relieved ascend to God on behalf of their benefactors. Keep the language of that third item concrete -- a subjection openly testified by their actions, and toward all men who stand in need. Then identify the exceeding grace of God said to be in them, and do not let it float free: what is meant is the merciful and charitable disposition itself, as the whole chapter shows. Attribute it to its right source. They had the means of charity, but God had given the means; they had a feeling and charitable heart, but God was the author of it; their charity was superabundant, and God furnished the disposition, the occasion, and the means by which the disposition was made manifest.

debates.question: What does the word for this service bring with it?

sides.position: Public service to the State in classical Greek, the ritual services of tabernacle and temple in the Greek Old Testament, and at first only the celebration of the Lord's Supper in church use, whence a liberal gift to Christ's poor is the most acceptable form of that service
Public service either in worship to God or in benefaction to others; our word liturgy is this word
Both the sacrifices and duties of priests and Levites, and the Athenian public offices discharged by the richest citizens at their own expense in rotation
That this is to be regarded not merely as an act of humanity but of religion

outliers.note: Alone turns the closing motive into a maxim about money, that the prayers of the poorest Christian are worth more than what is usually bestowed on him in charity, so that a man who has secured the pleadings of a humble child of God has made good use of his money.
Alone states what the collection was expected to demonstrate at Jerusalem, that Gentiles make as good Christians as Jews, remarking that actions speak louder than words.

themes: the administration of this service not only supplieth the want of the saints, but is abundant also by many thanksgivings unto God
they glorify God for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ
by their prayer for you, which long after you for the exceeding grace of God in you

15.pericope_label: Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift

schools.summary: Refuse the suggestion that this praise is for the charitable disposition the Corinthians had shown; it falls far below the design of the passage. The reference is to the Son given for them, and the abruptness is itself the evidence -- a mind so full of that subject that wherever Paul began he was sure to end at the Redeemer, the gift so familiar to his private thoughts that the remotest allusion turned him toward it. Still, be honest that the reference is inferred and not stated: the usage of the word elsewhere in Acts would favour the gift of the Spirit, and in Romans the gift of pardon, and it probably never entered the apostle's mind to subject a jubilant utterance of praise to minute analysis. Note the form of the sentence as well. This is the third thanksgiving in five verses, a gem flashed out after a tangled passage like a gleam of light clearing the air; the adjective appears nowhere else outside later church writers, and may have been coined here. And read the abruptness as a fact about dictation -- there was manifestly a pause at this point, in which thoughts of a very different kind began working, before he broke silence and began again.

Argue the reference from the previous verse rather than from sentiment. The unspeakable gift is precisely the same thing as the superabounding grace just named; that grace was evidently the work of Christ in them and not Christ himself; therefore what is praised here is the work and not the operator. Grant freely what the other reading has in its favour -- the Son given in God's love to mankind is an unspeakable blessing, and no man can conceive, much less declare, how great that gift is, since these are things the angels desire to look into -- and deny only that it is what this verse means. Then say why the work deserves the same word: the conversion of a soul from darkness to light is no less inconceivable, being a new creation, and creative energy cannot be comprehended. Or take the widest reading and leave the question open, the outward and inward blessings together, whose number and excellence cannot be uttered.

Offer the readings in succession without forcing a choice. It may mean the goodness of God shown to giver and receiver alike, since the one gave so liberally and the other received so largely only because God inclines the hearts of his children and provides for the needy. It may mean the exceeding grace bestowed on the Corinthians in their effectual calling. Or it may mean Christ himself, who is beyond question the unspeakable gift: though God's own Son, his only begotten, the Son of his love, his heir, he was given to be a covenant to the people, the head of the church, the Saviour of sinners, and a sacrifice in their room and stead. None can tell how great that gift is, so suitable and seasonable, so large and comprehensive, nor declare the love of Father and Son expressed in it. Whichever is meant, the duty is the same, and it is thankfulness.

sides.position: The Son given to die for them. The suggestion that it means the Corinthians' charitable disposition falls far below the design of the passage, and the abruptness shows a mind that ended at the Redeemer wherever it began
Not Christ himself but the work of Christ in them, since this phrase answers exactly to the superabounding grace of the previous verse, which was plainly that work and not the person

Left to conjecture. The usage in Acts favours the gift of the Spirit and that in Romans the gift of pardon, and it probably never entered Paul's thoughts to subject a jubilant utterance of praise to minute analysis
Any of three: the goodness of God to giver and receiver, the exceeding grace of their effectual calling, or Christ himself, who is beyond question an unspeakable gift
The outward and inward blessings together, whose number and excellence cannot be uttered

outliers.note: Alone argues against referring the unspeakable gift to Christ himself, on the ground that the phrase answers exactly to the superabounding grace of the previous verse, which was the work of Christ in them rather than the person.

Alone reads the abruptness as a fact about the dictation, holding that there was manifestly a pause here in which thoughts of a very different kind began working before the apostle broke silence and began anew.

themes: Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift
